title: An Analysis of Undergraduate Core Material in the Light of Hand-Held Computer Algebra Systems hand-held-computer-algebra-systems/ -- original paper:
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Pointon and Sangwin's 2003 analysis of undergraduate mathematics coursework, examining how vulnerable core assessment questions are to hand-held computer algebra systems (CAS) that can solve routine calculations automatically. The authors built an eight-category question taxonomy — spanning factual recall, routine calculation, classification, interpretation, proof, concept extension, example construction, and fallacy critique — and applied it, with inter-rater reliability checks, to real coursework. The headline finding is stark: three out of every five questions in the assessed material required nothing more than a routine calculation or algorithm, the exact category a hand-held CAS device can execute with minimal understanding. That means a student equipped with such a device could plausibly earn respectable marks on much of the coursework without engaging in real mathematical thinking. Although the technology examined dates to 2003, Barton highlights the taxonomy itself as the paper's most durable contribution: a practical tool teachers can use today to audit their own questions and check whether assessments are actually probing understanding rather than routine procedure — a question made sharply more urgent by modern AI tools that can solve routine calculations even more easily than dedicated CAS hardware ever could.
points: Three in five questions in the assessed undergraduate coursework required only a routine calculation or algorithm — precisely the category a hand-held CAS device can execute without genuine mathematical understanding.

The paper's eight-category question taxonomy (factual recall, routine calculation, classification, interpretation, proof, concept extension, example construction, fallacy critique) gives teachers a practical tool to audit their own assessment questions.
Surreptitious use of computational tools can let students earn respectable marks with 'little or no mental effort,' undermining the educational intent of an assessment even when scores look fine.
The taxonomy was validated through inter-rater reliability testing, giving it more credibility as a genuinely usable classification scheme rather than an ad hoc list.

Though the original technology (2003-era hand-held CAS) is dated, the underlying question — how much of an assessment tests routine procedure versus genuine understanding — is arguably more urgent now that modern AI tools can solve routine questions instantly.
quotes: This 2003 study from the International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology analyzes the impact of hand-held computer algebra systems (CAS) on undergraduate mathematics coursework.
The authors developed a question classification scheme to examine core mathematics courses, finding that a significant portion of tasks could be solved directly using CAS.
Their research highlights the potential for surreptitious CAS use to undermine the educational intent of assessments and proposes the classification scheme as a tool for improving assessment design.
The findings reveal a heavy reliance on routine calculations in the assessed coursework and suggest potential adjustments to assessment strategies in light of readily available CAS technology.
Taking the data set as a whole, the majority — three questions in five — require only routine calculations.
It would be tempting to conclude that a student equipped with one of these hand-held CAS would thus be able to obtain very respectable marks with little or no mental effort.
